Pentaho Server: The heart of the Business Analytics suite — the back-end that processes reporting, analysis, and dashboard content, hosts the central Repository, and provides scheduling and security. Business users reach it through the browser-based User Console.
Pentaho User Console: The browser-based home of the Pentaho Server, usually shortened to PUC. It is where business users log in to open and create reports, browse data sources, organise content, and manage schedules without installing anything on their machine.
Perspective: One of the task-oriented views the User Console is organised into — Home, Browse Files, Schedules, Administration, and so on. Perspectives group features by what a user is trying to do rather than mirroring the server's folder layout.
Browse Files: The User Console perspective for finding and managing content. The left pane lists folders (your personal home plus shared public space), the middle shows the files in the selected folder, and the Actions pane offers things like open, schedule, or add to favourites.
Repository: The Pentaho Server's central, secured store for all solution content — reports, analyses, dashboards, and data sources. Saving to it makes content discoverable and runnable by other users, subject to their permissions.
Schedule: A saved instruction to run a report automatically on a cadence (for example, emailing the EMEA Quantity report to regional leads each month). Scheduling delivers the same parameterised view to a known audience without anyone running it by hand.
Role: A named set of permissions assigned to users (such as Administrator, Power User, or Business Analyst). Roles decide what each person can do — read content, schedule it, publish it, create it, or manage data sources.
Permission: An individual capability granted to a role, such as Read Content, Create Content, Publish Content, Schedule Content, or Manage Data Sources. Permissions are enforced on the server before content is returned, so they cannot be bypassed by a different client.
Row-level security: Showing users different subsets of the same query results based on their identity or role — for example, EMEA managers only seeing EMEA rows. Enforced once at the model layer so every report inherits it, rather than being re-coded in each report.
Steel Wheels: The fictional model-car company whose sample data ships with Pentaho. The course's reports, analyses, and dashboards are built against its Orders, Customer, and sales data so exercises feel like a real business.
Data source: A reusable, business-friendly abstraction over a database connection, metadata model, or OLAP schema. Reports and dashboards reference a data source rather than embedding data, so administrators can change the underlying connection without rewriting every report.
Metadata model: A curated layer that translates the physical database into business vocabulary — friendly field names like Sales Amount and Territory instead of joins, keys, and technical column names. Interactive Reports build on it so users never see the SQL.
Interactive Reports: Pentaho's tool, often shortened to PIR, for letting non-technical users build ad-hoc tabular and grouped reports against a curated metadata model — picking fields, filters, and groupings with no SQL and no IT round-trip.
Grouping: Collapsing a flat list into one section per value of a chosen dimension — for example, one section per Territory. Each group becomes a scannable block with its own header and aggregated measures.
Subtotal: An aggregated figure shown for each group in a report, such as total sales per Territory. Pairing grouping with subtotals turns raw rows into a business-ready, scannable layout.
Prompt: A run-time parameter that lets the consumer pick a value — for example, Year equals 2024 or Region equals EMEA — so one report or dashboard definition can serve many scenarios instead of being rebuilt for each.
Computed field: A new field derived from existing ones inside a report, such as Margin equals Revenue minus Cost. It keeps authoring agile when the metadata team has not yet defined the measure you need.
Export: Saving a finished report out of the browser in a chosen format. CSV strips formatting for downstream tooling like Excel or scripts, while PDF preserves the visual layout for human reading.
Analyzer: Pentaho's web-based OLAP analysis tool, often shortened to PAZ. Its drag-and-drop pivot lets business users slice, dice, drill, and pivot multidimensional data and build charts without writing queries.
OLAP: Online Analytical Processing — pre-modelling data as cubes of dimensions, hierarchies, and measures so users can drill, slice, and pivot at speed. A cube is queried instead of reading raw rows, which is what makes Analyzer's interactions fast and intuitive.
Dimension: A descriptive axis you analyse data by — Time, Territory, Product Line, Customer. Dimensions are the ways you can slice and group the measures in a cube.
Hierarchy: An ordered set of levels within a dimension, such as Country then Region then City, or Year then Quarter then Month. Hierarchies give Analyzer its navigation skeleton, enabling drill-down and automatic roll-ups at each level.
Measure: A numeric value being analysed, such as Sales Amount or Quantity. Measures are aggregated automatically as you drill up and down a hierarchy.
Calculated measure: A measure derived from others — for example, Margin percent equals Revenue divided by Cost minus one. Defining it once at the cube means every Analyzer view, dashboard, and dependent report inherits the same definition.
Drill-down: Moving from a higher level of a hierarchy to the next level below on the same measure — for example, from Year to Quarter — while the rest of the context stays put. Drill-up does the reverse.
Drill-through: Clicking an aggregated cell to reveal the underlying detail rows that produced it. Where OLAP excels at the how much, drill-through answers which records without leaving the tool.
Slicing: Pinning one dimension to a value or set — such as Year equals 2024 — while letting the other dimensions vary. Dicing is the related move that pins several dimensions at once.
Pivoting: Reorganising how dimensions lay out in the grid — for example, moving Year from rows to columns. It surfaces patterns the original orientation hid, without changing the data or the filters.
Conditional formatting: Applying visual cues to a measure — such as red when revenue falls below target — so consumers spot exceptions at a glance instead of reading every number. It changes the display, never the underlying data.
Visualisation: A chart or graphical view of data — bar, line, treemap, geo map, scatter, and so on. The right type follows the question being asked: bars for comparison, lines for trend, treemaps for hierarchical proportion.
Treemap: A visualisation that encodes the relative size of nested categories using area — for example, quantity sold per Territory within EMEA — making part-of-whole relationships visible at a glance.
Mondrian: Pentaho's OLAP engine, also called the Analysis Schema layer. It defines dimensions, hierarchies, and measures on top of a relational warehouse and translates the user's intuitive MDX queries into efficient SQL on demand.
MDX: Multidimensional Expressions — the query language used to interrogate OLAP cubes. Analyzer generates MDX behind the scenes as you drill and pivot, and Mondrian converts it into SQL against the underlying database.
Dashboard Designer: Pentaho's tool, often shortened to PDD, for composing multiple reports, charts, and prompts onto one page so a consumer sees a connected view of an area of the business at a glance.
Dashboard: A single page that composes several visualisations and prompts together, often wired to shared filters, so one selection updates every panel and the consumer compares views that are always consistent.
Panel: An individual content area within a dashboard layout that holds one report, chart, or visualisation. Panels can be resized and arranged using layout templates such as the 2 over 1 configuration.
Layout template: A predefined arrangement of panels you pick when building a dashboard — for example, 2 over 1 — that establishes the visual foundation, to which you then apply a theme such as Ruby and add content.
Dashboard prompt: A shared control on a dashboard — a button group, drop-down, list, radio button, checkbox, or date picker — that filters multiple panels at once by feeding values into each report's parameters, keeping every panel in sync.
Metadata list: A prompt data option that pulls its values from a defined data source rather than a typed static list — for example, querying the Orders source for the list of Territories, optionally excluding null values.
Self-service BI: A model where curated end users author their own ad-hoc views against governed data models, as opposed to managed reporting, where IT builds the reports and consumers only read them. Both flow from the same governed models.
